 Her Late Father May Have Money Sitting With the State Right Now. Finding It Takes One Search, and Claiming It Costs Nothing
 States are sitting on billions in forgotten accounts, uncashed checks, and old benefits that legally belong to heirs, and most families never think to look. A few targeted searches could turn up a late parent's name attached to money no…
 By David Beren 
 Published November 1, 2026, 2:04pm ET · 4 min read 
 Life After Work desk. Editor: David Beren .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 NAUPA estimates roughly 1 in 7 people have unclaimed cash or property waiting, and searching or claiming it through official state programs costs nothing.
 A full search covers MissingMoney.com, each state's site, PBGC pensions, the Labor Department's lost retirement database, and IRS tax refunds.
 Tax refund claims carry a federal deadline: file within 3 years of the return or 2 years from when the tax was paid, whichever is later.

 Searching a late father’s name on a state unclaimed property website can uncover a forgotten bank balance or an uncashed paycheck in his name. States hold this money for owners and their heirs. Searching for a dead parent’s unclaimed money and claiming it through the state’s official program costs nothing. The National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators (NAUPA) estimates that approximately 1 in 7 people have unclaimed cash or property waiting.
 How a Father’s Old Account Ends Up With the State
 Unclaimed property is money a company owes someone but couldn’t deliver. NAUPA says it includes billions in uncashed payroll checks, stocks, credit balances, and more, and USA.gov lists bank accounts, insurance policies, or state agencies as common sources. When an account sits untouched long enough (a stretch called the dormancy period), the business reports it and turns it over to the state. The state holds the money until the owner or a legal heir comes forward. Common types of unclaimed property include uncashed paychecks, bank accounts, stocks, credit balances, and insurance benefits.
 Why Claiming Costs Nothing
 NAUPA, an affiliate network of the National Association of State Treasurers, says “Both searching for and claiming your unclaimed property are free, provided you go through the official government program of the state holding the property.” It notes that when a state search finds a match, there is no fee to claim the property.
 Searching Every State He Lived or Worked In
 USA.gov says unclaimed money is spread across separate databases, so a full search takes a few steps.
 A common starting point is MissingMoney.com, a free site for searching unclaimed property databases for participating states. Most states participate, but some of the biggest, including California and New York, may require a separate search on their official sites. NAUPA’s site, unclaimed.org, has a map linking to each state’s official program.
 You can repeat the search in every state where he lived or worked. USA.gov tells people who have lived in other states to check their unclaimed property offices, too. An old employer or bank elsewhere can mean money sits in another state’s records.
 Old pensions are another source. The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) holds benefits that went unpaid when a private-sector plan ended. Its search asks for a last name and the last four digits of your Social Security number, and PBGC says a match is only a first step, followed by a call to confirm details.
 Another resource is the Department of Labor’s Retirement Savings Lost and Found Database, created through the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022. It helps people find plans that may still owe benefits. The Labor Department says it’s an information database only and doesn’t pay benefits.
 Savings bonds can also be checked. TreasuryDirect says its Treasury Hunt tool has been unavailable since September 30, 2025, and now directs people with lost, stolen, or destroyed bonds to its forms page to file a claim.
 A tax refund may also be owed but not filed. Under the IRS Form 1040 instructions, a surviving spouse filing jointly just files the return, a court-appointed representative attaches proof of appointment, and all other filers requesting the deceased taxpayer’s refund must file the return and attach Form 1310.
 What an Heir Has to Prove
 NAUPA requires proof of ownership for every claim. For an heir, that means showing the owner died and that the claimant has a legal right to the money. Each state sets its own document list. The state’s claim page lists what it wants.
 Finder Fees and Time Limits That Cost Families Money
 So-called finders, also known as locators or heir finders, contact families and offer to get back unclaimed money for a percentage of it. Some states regulate these deals. California’s Code of Civil Procedure Section 1582 voids any agreement that requires the owner to pay a fee or compensation before the state approves the claim and makes payment. A valid California agreement must include the address where the owner can file a claim directly, and the fee can’t exceed 10% of the recovered property. Rules differ elsewhere, and because the state’s own claim process is free, an upfront payment request is a warning sign.
 Tax refunds also come with a time limit. Under 26 U.S.C. § 6511(a), a refund claim generally has to be filed within 3 years from the time the return was filed or 2 years from the time the tax was paid, whichever of such periods expires the later.
 One Search Worth Running
 A first search needs only a name and a state. Searches for each family member who has died, in every state they called home, cover the most ground, and the official state sites charge nothing to search or to claim.
